newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore gas oil upside capped by prompt supplies.
newsitem.headline: Singapore gas oil upside capped by prompt supplies.

text.p: Singapore gas oil is looking to fresh demand from India and China to lift the market but persistent offers of prompt cargoes in the physical market by one trader is expected to cap any rises, traders said on Wednesday.
"The market should pick up at the end of this week or next week as there are some new regional demand but there are alot of physical offers," one trader said.
Traders said the Singapore market is weighed down by offers from a local trader who had since mid-January sold a total of seven 150,000-190,000-barrel cargoes.
The trader had earlier imported 440,000-tonnes of gas oil from the Middle East for sale to China but Chinese buying has ground to a halt since mid-January.
"We bought the cargoes to sell to China but now we are stuck. We still have cargoes to sell," the trader said.
As a result of the traders' predicament, most players said it would be difficult for gas oil to rise substantially.

The Singapore gas oil market was boosted by news of a 50,000-tonne sale recently to a trader to cover committments to India--the first time in months that cargoes from Singapore were used to cover Indian Oil Corp's (IOC) monthly requirement.
Sources said low prices in Singapore made it viable for traders to cover their March shorts to IOC for delivery to the Indian east coast from Singapore.
Gas oil prices in Singapore have over the past few weeks traded within a $25.00-$25.50 per barrel range after falling from a peak of $34.45 per barrel in early December.
In addition to short coverings to India, players are also optimistic of a rebound as China had put out feelers to buy cargoes for late February and March arrival.
China bought a record one million tonnes of gas oil for December arrival which sent prices soaring but it subsequently more than halved purchases for January and February delivery.
On the eve of the Lunar New Year, China bought a 30,000-tonne cargo for end February arrival at $1.20 per barrel over Singapore spot quotes on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) basis.
Prior to that it bought one or two cargoes at $203-205 per tonne c-and-f south China basis and is currently indicating at around $195-198 per tonne.

As buyers are still away for the holidays gas oil stocks in Hong Kong remain high and prices have edged down. On an ex-terminal basis cargoes are currently offered at $203-205 per tonne and "business is slow", one trader said.
But many are confident that China will firm up its buying interest towards the end of this week for both barge and cargo lots.
